explanations.explanation: Signs it is. Nicodemus, a Pharisee and a leader of the Jews, says, “For no one could perform the signs You are doing if God were not with him.” He's telling Jesus what he has noticed and what he thinks it means. I think the man did his homework before he ever knocked on the door.

Nicodemus never says a word about sacrifices. He says, “For no one could perform the signs You are doing if God were not with him.” The signs are what he has seen Jesus doing. Sacrifices belong to a whole different conversation, friend.

I get why ceremonies sounds right, since it has that official ring to it. But Nicodemus says, “For no one could perform the signs You are doing if God were not with him.” He's talking about what Jesus is doing, not about anything with a ribbon to cut. Signs is the word.

That's the one. Nicodemus asks, “Can he enter his mother’s womb a second time to be born?” He starts with “How can a man be born when he is old?” I think he's picturing it exactly as Jesus said it, and honestly, that picture makes me want to sit down.

A father's house is a nice place to go back to, but Nicodemus never mentions it. He says, “Can he enter his mother’s womb a second time to be born?” The question is about being born again, so he's talking about where birth happens. That's why his father's house doesn't fit.

Going back to your hometown sounds like a fine weekend trip, but it's not what Nicodemus asks about. He says, “Can he enter his mother’s womb a second time to be born?” That's the picture he's stuck on. No hometown anywhere in that question.

Amazed is right. Jesus says, “Do not be amazed that I said, ‘You must be born again.’” He says it right after talking about being born of the Spirit. Jesus is calming the moment down, and I think a little amazement is understandable.
The text doesn't say Nicodemus was angry. Jesus tells him, “Do not be amazed that I said, ‘You must be born again.’” The word Jesus uses is amazed. Nobody slams a door in this scene.
Nothing in the text says Nicodemus was ashamed. Jesus says, “Do not be amazed that I said, ‘You must be born again.’” That's amazed, not ashamed. Those two words just look like cousins.

Yes, you hear it. Jesus says, “You hear its sound, but you do not know where it comes from or where it is going.” The sound shows up even when the rest stays a mystery. Wind works like that on a cooling rack too: you notice it before you see it.

explanations.answer: You know where it comes from
explanations.explanation: Jesus says the opposite. “You hear its sound, but you do not know where it comes from or where it is going.” Where the wind comes from is exactly what you don't know. I've stood in the bakery doorway trying to guess, and it never helped.

explanations.answer: You know where it is going
explanations.explanation: That's the other thing Jesus says you don't know. “You hear its sound, but you do not know where it comes from or where it is going.” The wind blows where it wishes. Following it would be a very long walk, friend.

True. Jesus says the wind blows where it wishes, then adds, “So it is with everyone born of the Spirit.” The wind is His picture for them. And Nicodemus asked about being born, so Jesus gave him something he could hear.

It's actually true. After talking about the wind, Jesus says, “So it is with everyone born of the Spirit.” The wind is the picture He uses for them. It's the same sentence that ends the thought, so it's easy to blow right past.

Israel's teacher, that's the title. Jesus says, “You are Israel’s teacher,” and then asks if he does not understand these things. It's a big title to be handed right before a question like that. I'd feel the weight of it for sure.

Jesus doesn't call Nicodemus a priest. The text says Nicodemus is a Pharisee and a leader of the Jews, and Jesus says, “You are Israel’s teacher.” Teacher is the title on the table. The temple just isn't part of this one.
That title never comes up. What Jesus says is, “You are Israel’s teacher.” Nicodemus is a Pharisee and a leader of the Jews, but nobody here calls him a judge. Teacher is the one Jesus picks.
It's the other way around. Jesus says, “…and yet you people do not accept our testimony.” That's a real moment of honesty in the conversation. So the statement on the card is false.

Right, it's false. Jesus says, “…and yet you people do not accept our testimony.” He says that straight after talking about what they have seen. That's the text's own wording, so we leave it just as it is.

Heavenly things. Jesus says, “If I have told you about earthly things and you do not believe, how will you believe if I tell you about heavenly things?” He's asking about the next step up. And I'm still working on the earthly ones myself.

Jesus doesn't bring up the prophets here. He says, “If I have told you about earthly things and you do not believe, how will you believe if I tell you about heavenly things?” Heavenly things are the harder part. The prophets just aren't in that sentence.

The law of Moses isn't in this verse. Jesus says, “If I have told you about earthly things and you do not believe, how will you believe if I tell you about heavenly things?” Moses does show up a couple of verses later. Right here it's heavenly things.

Yes, the Son of Man. Jesus says, “Just as Moses lifted up the snake in the wilderness, so the Son of Man must be lifted up.” Moses, Israel's leader, is the one who lifted the snake. And Son of Man is the name Jesus uses for Himself (Mark 2:10).

The temple isn't what Jesus mentions. He says, “Just as Moses lifted up the snake in the wilderness, so the Son of Man must be lifted up.” Moses, Israel's leader, lifted the snake. Jesus pairs it with the Son of Man, which is the name He uses for Himself (Mark 2:10).

Moses is in the sentence, but his law isn't. Jesus says, “Just as Moses lifted up the snake in the wilderness, so the Son of Man must be lifted up.” Moses was Israel's leader, and he's the one who lifted the snake. Jesus is the Son of Man, the name He uses for Himself (Mark 2:10).
Eternal life. Jesus says it's “that everyone who believes in Him may have eternal life.” Everyone who believes, no list of exceptions attached. That's a big word, friend, and it's the word He uses.

Earthly does show up in the conversation, back in verse 12, where Jesus talks about earthly things. But here He says, “that everyone who believes in Him may have eternal life.” This verse is about the life He gives. Eternal is the word.
Peaceful sounds lovely, but it isn't the word here. Jesus says, “that everyone who believes in Him may have eternal life.” That's the life He's talking about. Nothing about a quiet afternoon in it.

explanations.answer: To save the world through Him
explanations.explanation: That's it. Jesus says, “For God did not send His Son into the world to condemn the world, but to save the world through Him.” First what He didn't come to do, then what He did. Short and clear, my favorite kind of teaching.

explanations.answer: To give the world a new law
explanations.explanation: A new law isn't what the verse says. Jesus says, “For God did not send His Son into the world to condemn the world, but to save the world through Him.” The reason is saving, and it's through the Son. No new rulebook in sight.

explanations.answer: To rebuild the temple in Jerusalem
explanations.explanation: Rebuilding the temple isn't mentioned here. Jesus says, “For God did not send His Son into the world to condemn the world, but to save the world through Him.” That's the reason, right there in plain words. No construction crew required.

True. Jesus says, “…whoever does not believe has already been condemned, because he has not believed in the name of God’s one and only Son.” He says it plainly. This is one of those lines I read slowly.

It's true, and it's a tough one. Jesus says, “…whoever does not believe has already been condemned, because he has not believed in the name of God’s one and only Son.” Those are His words. So the card holds up.

Yes. Jesus says, “The Light has come into the world, but men loved the darkness rather than the Light.” It's a heavy line, and I won't pretend otherwise. Light came, and that's how people answered it.

explanations.answer: They gave thanks for the Light
explanations.explanation: That's not what Jesus says. He says, “The Light has come into the world, but men loved the darkness rather than the Light.” The word is loved, and it's pointed at the darkness. It's a hard verse.

explanations.answer: They waited for a greater sign
explanations.explanation: Waiting for a bigger sign isn't in this verse. Jesus says, “The Light has come into the world, but men loved the darkness rather than the Light.” That's the response He names. Nobody's holding out for more.
Deeds. Jesus says men loved the darkness rather than the Light “because their deeds were evil.” That's the reason He gives. And to be clear, He's the one giving it.
Rulers are never named in this verse. Jesus says men loved the darkness rather than the Light “because their deeds were evil.” It's the deeds He points to. Keep an eye on that word as you read on.
Neighbors aren't in this verse at all. Jesus says men loved the darkness rather than the Light “because their deeds were evil.” The word is deeds. Nobody gets blamed on the block.

explanations.answer: He fears his deeds will be exposed
explanations.explanation: That's the reason. Jesus says, “Everyone who does evil hates the Light, and does not come into the Light for fear that his deeds will be exposed.” The fear is about what the Light would show. Think of someone not wanting the kitchen light on at 2 a.m. when the cookie jar is half empty.

explanations.answer: He thinks the Light is too far away
explanations.explanation: Distance isn't the issue in this verse. Jesus says, “Everyone who does evil hates the Light, and does not come into the Light for fear that his deeds will be exposed.” The reason is the fear of exposure. The Light isn't described as far off.

explanations.answer: He is waiting for someone to lead him
explanations.explanation: Waiting for a guide isn't what Jesus says. He says, “Everyone who does evil hates the Light, and does not come into the Light for fear that his deeds will be exposed.” That fear is the reason given. No tour guide mentioned.
It's the opposite. Jesus says, “But whoever practices the truth comes into the Light.” That's who walks toward it. So the card is false.

Right, false. Jesus says, “But whoever practices the truth comes into the Light, so that it may be seen clearly that what he has done has been accomplished in God.” They come toward the Light and don't stay away. It's a nice way to end the conversation.
